title: Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
description: How reinforcement learning turns a pre-trained, supervised-tuned LLM into an aligned reasoning model: RLHF, PPO, DPO, GRPO and successors, reward and verifier design, RL environments, and when to use which method.

modules.title: The RL Post-Training Loop as a Cost Model: Rollout, Reward, Update, and Where the GPU-Hours Go
modules.description: What one RL iteration does to a GPU cluster, with the reported arithmetic (R1-Zero, Olmo 3, MiniMax-M1, ScaleRL) that every later module refers back to.

After this module the reader can estimate, from batch size, response length and engine throughput, which phase of an RL run is the bottleneck and what a run costs, and can read any later report's 'steps' and 'GPU-hours' figures critically. Derived arithmetic is shown and marked as derived.
topics: post-training map: pretrain -> SFT -> preference tuning (RLHF with PPO, or DPO) -> RLVR/agentic RL -> distillation; which stages sample from the current policy (on-policy) and which train on fixed data; where this course starts relative to SFT (Lambert ch. 3)

modules.title: Policy Gradients for Token Sequences: the Log-Derivative Trick, Baselines, and Advantages for an LLM Policy
modules.description: Derives the policy-gradient estimator for an autoregressive policy under both the token-MDP and one-action-per-completion views, and why every later algorithm is a variance, bias or step-size fix to it.
modules.scope: In: LLM generation as an MDP (state = prompt + prefix, action = next token, deterministic transition, reward at the last token) and as a contextual bandit (the whole completion is one action), as used by InstructGPT and argued for by the REINFORCE-for-RLHF paper; the log-derivative trick and the sequence-level score function; REINFORCE as reward-weighted SFT on the policy's own samples (a bridge from SFT, which he knows); baselines as variance reducers that leave the gradient unbiased; advantage; value functions and why a per-token value is hard when reward arrives only at the last token; on-policy sampling and the importance-sampling correction (stated, used in Module 3); why sparse binary rewards need nonzero pass rate to learn. Out: trust regions and PPO (Module 3), group baselines (Module 9), KL (Module 6). After this module the reader can derive the policy gradient for a sequence model, write REINFORCE with a baseline, and classify any later algorithm by where it gets its baseline and how it limits step size. Sutton & Barto chapter and page numbers come from search-result summaries only (S5 not fetched): mark them unverified.

modules.title: From TRPO to PPO: Trust Regions, Importance Ratios, the Clipped Surrogate, and GAE
modules.description: The lineage Aman asked about, cited correctly: Schulman et al.'s TRPO (2015), GAE (2016) and PPO (2017), what each constraint does, and which pieces GRPO later keeps.
modules.scope: In: why plain policy-gradient steps are unsafe; TRPO's monotonic-improvement theory, the move from a total-variation penalty to an average-KL constraint (delta = 0.01), conjugate gradient plus line search, single-path vs vine sampling, kinship with natural gradient; PPO's ratio, the clipped objective L^CLIP with epsilon = 0.2, the min as a pessimistic bound, multiple minibatch epochs, the adaptive-KL variant that did worse, MuJoCo hyperparameters (Table 3); GAE (gamma, lambda, bias-variance); what clipping does not guarantee (it does not bound KL; clipping bias that amplifies high-prior behaviours); the TRPO -> PPO -> GRPO lineage map. This module also corrects the request: DeepSeek-R1 uses GRPO (introduced in DeepSeekMath, Feb 2024), not TRPO. Out: the LLM-specific PPO system (Module 5), GRPO (Module 9). After this module the reader can derive the clipped-objective gradient for A>0 and A<0, say exactly which trust-region property PPO keeps and drops, and compute a GAE advantage by hand. Any claim that TRPO is 'impractical for LLMs' is the writer's reasoning, not a sourced fact: label it.

modules.title: KL Regularization and Reward-Model Over-Optimization: Reference Policies, the k1/k2/k3 Estimators, and Gold-versus-Proxy Scaling Laws
modules.description: Why a KL leash exists, how it is estimated from samples (and when the estimator's gradient is biased), and what the gold-vs-proxy scaling laws say about how far to optimise a proxy reward.
modules.scope: In: the KL-regularized RL objective and its closed-form optimum pi* proportional to pi_ref * exp(r/beta); the three sampled estimators k1, k2, k3 with Schulman's numbers (true KL 0.005 and 0.5: bias and standard deviation per estimator) and the reverse-direction estimator; KL in the reward (InstructGPT/PPO) vs KL in the loss (GRPO), and what that does to the advantage; the biased-gradient problem of k3 when sampled tokens are far less probable under pi_theta than pi_ref and DeepSeek-V3.2's importance-ratio fix; Gao et al.'s gold-vs-proxy design (proxy RMs 3M-3B, gold 6B InstructGPT RM), the functional forms in d = sqrt(KL) for best-of-n and RL, and why KL is a poor common yardstick; the KL coefficient across reports (R1 0.001, DeepSeekMath 0.04, Tulu 3 0.05-0.07, TRL default 0.0). Out: whether to keep KL in long-CoT RL (Module 13), reward hacking in verifiable and agentic settings (Module 19). After this module the reader can choose and implement a KL estimator for a given placement and explain what a KL budget buys.
topics: KL-regularized objective: maximise E[r] - beta * KL(pi || pi_ref); closed-form optimum pi* proportional to pi_ref * exp(r / beta) (derived; reused in Module 7)

GRPO objective: for each question sample G outputs from pi_old, advantage A_i = (r_i - mean(r))/std(r), per-token ratio and clip, KL term in the loss; why group-relative advantages match how RMs are trained
KL in the loss vs in the reward: consequence that KL does not enter the advantage; DeepSeekMath's unbiased KL estimator

DeepSeekMath-RL setup and results: lr 1e-6, KL 0.04, 64 outputs, max length 1024, batch 1024, one update per exploration stage (so the ratio is 1 and clipping is inert), ~144K CoT questions; GSM8K 82.9 -> 88.2, MATH 46.8 -> 51.7
outcome vs process supervision inside GRPO; iterative GRPO with 10% historical replay and reference resets
Online RFT vs GRPO: GRPO's gradient coefficient scales with reward magnitude and penalizes wrong answers; Online RFT reinforces only correct ones
unified paradigm table: SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, GRPO as special cases of one gradient form (data source, reward, coefficient)
Kimi k1.5's objective: online policy mirror descent with the current model as reference, sampled-mean baseline approximating tau * log Z, squared-error surrogate; contrast with GRPO
the critic debate: no critic (REINFORCE/RLOO, GRPO, Kimi) vs a value model still carrying weight (Tulu 3 RM-initialised value; Xu et al.); VAPO and ReMax as pointer-only (fetch before citing)
TRL's GRPOTrainer as a reference implementation: num_generations default 8, group-std scaling default, KL beta default 0.0
disagreements: Critic or no critic: is a value model worth it? (primary)

modules.title: RL with Verifiable Rewards: Rule-Based Reward Design, Prompt Selection, and What R1-Zero Showed
modules.description: RLVR as the RLHF objective with the reward model replaced by a verifier: what verifiers exist, how rewards are composed, and how prompts are chosen so the signal is learnable.
modules.scope: In: Tulu 3's definition (RLHF objective with a verification function; constant reward if verified; coined Nov 2024, pre-dating R1) and its targets (GSM8K, MATH, IFEval-style constraints); R1-Zero's reward (accuracy + format, equal weight; no neural RM) and the language-consistency reward with its measured cost; verifier examples in the shipped environments (math answer matching, code tests, SQL result-set equality, constraint checkers); query-verifier selection (Qwen3's 3,995 pairs and four criteria, Olmo 3's offline filter dropping pass rate above 62.5%, K2's difficulty by SFT-model pass@k, k1.5's curriculum and prioritized sampling); base-model dependence (R1-Zero AIME 15.6 -> 77.9% in the v2/Nature version vs 71.0% in v1; template sensitivity; the 'aha moment' already present in V3-Base per Dr. GRPO); R1-Zero's own problems (readability, language mixing). Out: judge and rubric rewards (Module 16), environments (Module 17), reward hacking (Module 19), the sharpen-or-expand debate (Module 20), the full R1 recipe (Module 27). After this module the reader can design a rule-based reward and a prompt-selection filter for a new verifiable domain and name its failure modes.
topics: RLVR definition and provenance: Tulu 3 (22 Nov 2024) vs R1 (22 Jan 2025); the RLHF objective with the RM replaced by a verifier; constant reward on verification
what is verifiable: GSM8K/MATH answer matching, IFEval-style precise instruction following, code via tests, SQL via unordered result-set equality (NeMo Gym Bird SQL), games with +1/0/-1
R1-Zero reward composition: accuracy + format, equal weight; why neural reward models (outcome or process) were deliberately avoided; the 'think'/'answer' template as part of the environment
the language-consistency reward (fraction of target-language words in the CoT; Eq. 7) and its slight performance cost

prompt selection as signal design: Qwen3's four criteria (not used in cold start, learnable, as challenging as possible, broad coverage) and 3,995 pairs; Olmo 3's pass-rate > 62.5% offline filter; K2's SFT-model pass@k difficulty rule; k1.5's easy-first curriculum with prioritized sampling toward low success
binary vs graded rewards and what a group of all-pass or all-fail rollouts does (pointer to Module 11 on zero-variance groups)
base-model dependence: R1-Zero 15.6% -> 77.9% (v2) / 71.0% (v1); Qwen2.5 base improves ~60% without a template vs the R1 template; template mismatch can destroy reasoning before RL starts
where R1-Zero's gains come from: R1 attributes reflection to RL; Dr. GRPO finds the 'aha moment' in V3-Base (source-level conflict)
R1-Zero's problems that motivated the multi-stage R1 (poor readability, language mixing, narrow reasoning-only RL) and the contamination caveat that motivates Olmo 3's RL-Zero
Reasoning Gym as verifiable tasks with adjustable difficulty (pointer to Module 17)
disagreements: Learned reward models, verifiers, or generative/rubric judges? (position A, rule-based verifiers; full treatment in Module 16)
Source-level conflict (S15 vs S18): R1 attributes emergent reflection to RL; Dr. GRPO finds it already in V3-Base

modules.title: The GRPO Loss and Advantage Under the Microscope: Length Bias, Difficulty Bias, Token-Level Averaging, and Zero-Variance Groups
modules.description: What the per-sequence 1/|o| average and the std division do to per-token gradient weight, and the competing fixes in Dr. GRPO, DAPO, V3.2, Olmo 3 and ScaleRL.
modules.scope: In: derivation of per-token gradient weight under the original GRPO aggregation; Dr. GRPO's two diagnosed biases (response-level length bias from 1/|o_i|: shorter correct answers get larger updates and longer wrong answers are penalised less; question-level difficulty bias from dividing by group std) and its constant normalizer fix (43.3% AIME 2024 on a 7B base); DAPO's token-level loss and its ablation ladder on AIME24 avg@32 (30 -> 36 -> 38 -> 41 -> 42 -> 50), overlong filtering and soft punishment (16,384 + 4,096 cache), dynamic sampling that drops accuracy-0 or accuracy-1 groups; DeepSeek-V3.2 (advantage = R - mean(R)), OlmoRL (token-level, no std, zero-gradient filtering, active sampling), ScaleRL (prompt-level averaging, batch-level advantage normalization, zero-variance filtering, no-positive-resampling); TRL's loss_type and scale_rewards options; the claim that these choices mostly move efficiency, not the asymptote. Out: ratio clipping (Module 12), entropy dynamics (Module 13), scaling fits (Module 15). After this module the reader can compute the per-token weight under any aggregation and pick a normalization with the evidence in hand. The ablation numbers are from one base model (Qwen2.5-32B) and one benchmark: state that.
topics: per-token gradient weight under the original GRPO loss: (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t ...; derivation that a token in a long response gets less weight (derived)
response-level length bias (Dr. GRPO Section 3.1): why wrong responses grow longer; the same normalization predates GRPO in open-source PPO implementations
question-level difficulty bias: std division up-weights very easy and very hard prompts (derived weight curve in p = pass rate)
Dr. GRPO: constant normalizer (e.g. max length) and no std; 43.3% AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B and a minimalist recipe
DAPO token-level policy-gradient loss: sample-level averaging underweights long responses and cannot penalise gibberish in them; ablation ladder 30/36/38/41/42/50 on AIME24 avg@32

zero-variance groups: P(all-correct or all-wrong) = p^G + (1-p)^G (derived); DAPO's dynamic sampling (oversample, drop accuracy 0/1), Olmo 3's active sampling and zero-gradient filtering, ScaleRL's zero-variance filtering and no-positive-resampling
overlong reward shaping: overlong filtering vs soft overlong punishment (16,384 expected max + 4,096 cache = 20,480)
advantage without std: DeepSeek-V3.2 (R_i - mean(R)) and OlmoRL; what changes when update magnitude then depends on raw reward scale (TRL scale_rewards note)
ScaleRL's position: prompt-level loss averaging and batch-level advantage normalization; loss aggregation and normalization mostly change compute efficiency, not asymptote
TRL options as a map of the debate: loss_type (grpo, dapo, dr_grpo), scale_rewards (group, batch, False), their defaults and what each reproduces
disagreements: How should the GRPO loss and advantage be normalized? (primary)
Controlling response length / reasoning effort (secondary: position D, fix the length bias in the loss rather than adding a penalty)

modules.title: Importance Ratios and Clipping: Token-Level, Sequence-Level (GSPO), IS-Weight Clipping (CISPO), and Log-Ratio Masks
modules.description: Why the PPO ratio is a different object in LLM RL than in MuJoCo, and the competing designs: Clip-Higher, GSPO, CISPO, Kimi's log-ratio mask, GLM-5's double-sided IS, V3.2's sequence masking.
modules.scope: In: when the ratio is non-trivial in LLM RL (DeepSeekMath's single update per exploration stage makes it 1; R1's 8,192-output rollout in 16 minibatches does not); GSPO's critique of token-level importance weights (one sample per position, variance growing with length, collapse), the sequence-level length-normalized ratio and its clip ranges (3e-4/4e-4 vs GRPO 0.2/0.27), Routing Replay needed by GRPO on MoE and not by GSPO; Clip-Higher (0.2/0.28); CISPO (stop-gradient clipped IS weight times a REINFORCE term, 'fork' tokens like However/Wait, 2x speedup vs DAPO at equal quality); Kimi K2.5's log-ratio mask independent of the sign of the advantage, K3's per-token regularization tolerance to staleness; GLM-5's direct double-sided importance sampling; DeepSeek-V3.2's off-policy sequence masking for negative-advantage sequences; SAPO's soft gate (pointer-only abstract, TRL implements it); R1's printed clip epsilon of 10 in stage-1 RL (unexplained: unverified). Out: numerical sources of off-policyness (Module 14) and infrastructure staleness (System Design course Module 37). After this module the reader can write each variant's loss, say which tokens receive gradient under each, and predict which variant tolerates MoE routing noise and stale rollouts.
topics: when the ratio matters: pi_theta / pi_old equals 1 for a single update per rollout (DeepSeekMath); with 16 minibatches per 8,192-output rollout (R1) later minibatches are off-policy by design (derived)

GSPO's diagnosis: token-level importance weights are a misapplication of importance sampling (one sample per token position); variance grows with length and is amplified by clipping, ending in irreversible collapse
GSPO: sequence-likelihood ratio with length normalization, clipped at the sequence level (Eq. 5); clip ranges 3e-4/4e-4 vs GRPO 0.2/0.27 because the log-ratio scale differs
MoE: GRPO needs Routing Replay to converge; GSPO removes the need because sequence likelihood is insensitive to which experts a token routed to; training/inference precision tolerance
Clip-Higher: eps_low 0.2, eps_high 0.28; why raising the lower bound would crush low-probability tokens to 0 and collapse the sampling space

CISPO (MiniMax-M1): clip the importance weight, not the update, with stop-gradient; rare 'fork' tokens (However, Recheck, Wait, Aha) get clipped out under PPO-style clipping; 2x speedup vs DAPO on Qwen2.5-32B
Kimi K2.5 token-level log-ratio mask [alpha, beta], independent of advantage sign; K3 per-token regularization as staleness tolerance
GLM-5 direct double-sided importance sampling: clip [1 - eps_l, 1 + eps_h] on rollout log-probs, no tracking of historical policy checkpoints
DeepSeek-V3.2 off-policy sequence masking: mask whole sequences with negative advantage whose policy divergence exceeds delta, measured with the inference engine's probabilities
SAPO soft temperature-controlled gate (pointer-only; TRL implements it) and the claim GSPO suppresses whole sequences for a few off-policy tokens
R1's printed 'GRPO clip ratio epsilon = 10' in stage-1 RL: unexplained, mark unverified; TRL epsilon/epsilon_high/CISPO defaults (0.2, 0.28 recommended, 5.0 for CISPO)
disagreements: Importance ratio and clipping: token-level, sequence-level, IS-weight clipping, or soft gating? (primary)

parts.title: Making RL Run: Dynamics, Numerical Mismatch, and Compute Scaling
parts.description: What goes wrong during long RL runs (entropy collapse, length drift, probability mismatch between inference and training engines) and what scaling studies say about compute.

modules.title: Training Dynamics: Entropy Collapse, KL Drift, Length Growth, and the Controls That Work
modules.description: The mechanism behind entropy collapse (a covariance between probability and advantage), the fixes proposed, and the keep-or-remove-KL disagreement for long-CoT RL.
modules.scope: In: the empirical entropy-performance law R = -a * exp(H) + b and its predictable ceiling; the covariance mechanism (entropy change tracks the covariance between action probability and logit change, i.e. advantage under policy gradient); Clip-Cov and KL-Cov; Clip-Higher and dynamic/active sampling; ProRL (KL penalty with periodic reference resets, higher temperature, 1.5B model, >2k steps, per-domain gains); temperature decay in Kimi K2; the KL debate (removed in DAPO, Olmo 3, GLM-5, TRL default; kept with resets in ProRL; domain-dependent in V3.2; R1 0.001 with reference replaced every 400 steps); response-length growth and language mixing as run-health signals. Out: how to control length on purpose (Module 23), the numerical source of off-policy drift (Module 14), whether gains are real (Module 20). After this module the reader can read a run's entropy, KL, length and clip-fraction curves and choose among the documented interventions with the evidence and its limits (single base models, single benchmarks) in view. Magistral (arXiv 2506.10910, same consensus as Olmo 3) is a pointer only.
topics: entropy collapse in practice: early collapse to an over-confident policy and saturating reward in runs without intervention
the empirical law R = -a * exp(H) + b: performance is traded from entropy, the ceiling at H = 0 is R = -a + b (derived reading of the fit)

the covariance mechanism: entropy change driven by covariance between action probability and the change in logits; high-probability high-advantage actions lower entropy, rare high-advantage actions raise it
Clip-Cov and KL-Cov: select the high-covariance tokens and clip or penalise only those
Clip-Higher and dynamic/active sampling as DAPO and Olmo 3's answer (position A); why the upper clip bound matters for low-probability tokens

ProRL: explicit KL with reference resets and higher temperature as a more stable entropy fix when starting from a distilled checkpoint; 'remove KL' advice said to apply to base models; gains (14.7% math, 13.9% coding, 54.8% logic, 25.1% STEM, 18.1% instruction following at pass@1)
temperature decay (Kimi K2): high early for exploration, lower later for reliability

KL handling across reports: DAPO/Olmo 3/GLM-5/TRL remove it; ProRL keeps it with resets; V3.2 domain-dependent with a corrected estimator; R1 0.001 and reference replaced every 400 steps; DeepSeekMath 0.04; Tulu 3 0.05/0.07
length and language drift as run-health signals: R1-Zero length growth (32,768 -> 65,536 max length at step 8.2k), mixing of languages, Dr. GRPO's length-bias account of growing wrong answers

a run-health dashboard assembled from what the reports track (entropy, KL, response length, clip fraction, zero-advantage fraction, reward) with the fix each report applied; no metric included that no report uses
disagreements: How to prevent entropy collapse (primary)
Keep or remove the KL-to-reference term? (primary for long-CoT RL)

modules.title: Training-Inference Mismatch: Why the Rollout Engine and the Trainer Disagree on Probabilities, and the Four Families of Fixes
modules.description: Why vLLM-style rollout probabilities differ from trainer probabilities for the same weights and what that does to the 'on-policy' assumption, with the numerical, statistical, deterministic and masking fixes reported.
modules.scope: In: sources of divergence for the same weights (kernel and precision differences, BF16 rounding, fused ops, top-p/top-k sampling masks, MoE routing, non-deterministic top-k in a sparse-attention indexer); why the 'on-policy' sample is silently off-policy and the 'deployment gap' (weights optimised for the training engine, not the serving engine); the four fix families with their costs: (A) statistical correction (truncated or masked importance sampling, token- vs sequence-level; roughly 25% extra training cost for the extra forward pass, as estimated in the FP16 paper), (B) numerics (MiniMax-M1's FP32 LM head, ScaleRL's FP32 logits, FP16 instead of BF16), (C) removing the source (V3.2's Keep Routing and Keep Sampling Mask; GLM-5's deterministic torch.topk plus IcePop), (D) masking off-policy sequences using the inference engine's probabilities; why hybrid-attention and MoE models are hit harder. Facts about Yao et al.'s TIS and Liu et al. are second-hand via S27/S48 (Notion pages unread): mark them. Out: infrastructure for weight sync and asynchronous staleness (System Design course Modules 37, 38). This is the module where Aman's inference background is the lever: he can reason about kernels, precision and sampling-path differences directly; the writer should use that, labelling analogies as the writer's own. After this module the reader can instrument a rollout/trainer pair to measure mismatch and pick a fix class for a given architecture.
topics: why two engines disagree on identical weights: reduction order and fused kernels, BF16 rounding, different attention backends, sampling truncation (top-p/top-k) altering the action space, MoE routing differences
consequence: the policy that generated the data is not the policy the trainer thinks it is; importance ratio is polluted; the deployment gap (weights optimised for the training engine's distribution)

measuring mismatch: per-token |log p_inference - log p_train|, correlation, token-level KL; MiniMax-M1's layer-by-layer trace to high-magnitude LM-head activations (correlation labelled 0.987319 after the FP32 head; text says it rose from roughly 0.9x)

family A, statistical: truncated IS (TIS), masked IS (MIS), sequence-level ratios; TRL's default sequence-level masked IS with TIS clip max 3.0; Olmo 3's truncated IS; Liu et al.'s unbiased sequence-level ratio and its variance; ~25% extra cost (second-hand, unverified)

family B, numerics: FP32 LM head (MiniMax-M1; mismatch absent in smaller dense softmax models, so architecture and kernel dependent), ScaleRL FP32 logits, FP16 vs BF16 ('a few lines of change'), and the root-cause disagreement between them

family C, remove the source: V3.2 Keep Routing (since V3-0324) and Keep Sampling Mask so pi_old and pi_theta share the action subspace; GLM-5's deterministic top-k fix (non-deterministic CUDA/TileLang top-k caused drastic degradation after a few steps with an entropy drop; torch.topk fixed it; indexer frozen; k = 2048 replay impractical)
family D, masking: V3.2 off-policy sequence masking from the inference engine's own probabilities; GSPO's tolerance claim; IcePop masking in GLM-5
why MoE and hybrid-attention architectures amplify the problem; token-in-token-out gateways that avoid re-tokenization mismatch (GLM-5 TITO) as the multi-turn analogue
decision procedure for a new architecture: measure, find the dominant source, pick the cheapest fix class; the cost of recomputing log-probs in the trainer (links to Module 1 arithmetic)
disagreements: Fixing the training-inference mismatch (vLLM/SGLang rollout vs trainer): algorithm, numerics, or determinism? (primary)

modules.title: RL Compute Scaling: Sigmoidal Fits, the ScaleRL Recipe, and What Longer Runs Actually Buy
modules.description: How to read RL training curves as compute-performance sigmoids, which design choices change the asymptote versus the efficiency, and the compute budgets reports actually spend.
modules.scope: In: ScaleRL's fitting framework (sigmoid of pass rate against log compute with asymptote A, efficiency B, midpoint C_mid) from a study of >400,000 GPU-hours; its three findings (recipes differ in asymptote; loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum and off-policy algorithm mostly change efficiency; stable recipes extrapolate from small runs); the ScaleRL recipe (PipelineRL asynchronous with max off-policyness k = 8, forced length interruptions, CISPO, prompt-level averaging, batch-level advantage normalization, FP32 logits, zero-variance filtering, no-positive-resampling); its validation (100,000 GPU-hours on an 8B dense model, 50,000 on a 17B x 16 MoE, extrapolated from fits to 50,000/16,000); PipelineRL vs PPO-off-policy; compute budgets in reports (R1-Zero ~3.75% of pretraining, V3.2 >10%, Kimi K3 on scaling RL FLOPs, MiniMax-M1's 3-week run); ProRL and DAPO's 'half the steps' claims; how to normalise 'steps' across reports. Out: infrastructure (System Design course), entropy and stability interventions (Module 13). After this module the reader can fit a saturating curve to a run's early data, say what is an efficiency improvement versus an asymptote improvement, and read any report's compute claim with the normalization it needs. The claim that RL compute rose >10x from o1 to o3 is the ScaleRL authors' citation, second-hand: mark it.
topics: the sigmoid framework: expected reward vs log(compute) with asymptote A, efficiency B, midpoint C_mid; why a sigmoid and what each parameter means
study scale and method: >400,000 GPU-hours, ablations on common design choices, fits from small runs extrapolated to large
three findings: asymptote differs by recipe; loss aggregation/normalization/curriculum/off-policy algorithm mostly change efficiency; stable recipes extrapolate

ScaleRL recipe components and the reason each is in it (PipelineRL k = 8, forced length interruptions, CISPO, prompt-level averaging, batch-level advantage normalization, FP32 logits, zero-variance filtering, no-positive-resampling)
validation runs: 100k GPU-hours on 8B dense and 50k on a 17B x 16 MoE, extrapolated from fits up to 50k and 16k
PipelineRL vs PPO-off-policy: similar asymptote, faster approach because of less idle time (links to Module 1)
compute budgets in reports side by side: R1-Zero ~100,000 H800 GPU-hours = 3.75% of pretraining; V3.2 >10%; MiniMax-M1 512 H800 x 3 weeks; Kimi K3's scaling-RL-FLOPs claim; Olmo 3 step time

efficiency claims in 'steps': DAPO 50 AIME points in 50% of the steps vs R1-Zero-Qwen-32B; CISPO matches DAPO with 50% of the steps; how a 'step' differs across reports (prompts x samples x length; derived normalization table)
prolonged-RL evidence (ProRL >2k steps) and how scaling studies relate to the sharpen-vs-expand debate (forward pointer to Module 20)
limits of the evidence: one model family per study, fitted not measured asymptotes, extrapolation horizons
disagreements: How should the GRPO loss and advantage be normalized? (position E: these choices move efficiency, not the asymptote)
Source-level conflict (S22 vs S45): RL at ~3.75% of pretraining compute vs >10%; different regimes, not a contradiction

parts.title: Rewards, Environments, Agents, and Their Failure Modes
parts.description: Where reward signals come from when a unit test is not enough, what an RL environment is, how multi-turn agent training differs, how rewards get exploited, and what the resulting numbers do and do not show.

modules.title: Rewards Beyond Ground Truth: LLM Judges, Rubric Rewards, Generative Reward Models, and Judges Trained Inside the Loop
modules.description: How 2025-2026 recipes get a reward signal for tasks with no verifier: rubrics, self-critic pairwise rewards, tournament-style judging, and generative reward models optimised jointly with the policy.
modules.scope: In: the verifier-to-judge ladder; Rubrics as Rewards (instance-specific rubrics; up to 31% relative on HealthBench vs a Likert judge; abstract-only in the source map, so fetch); Kimi K2's self-critic pairwise reward with closed-loop critic refinement on verifiable rollouts and a rubric attached to each synthesized task; K2.5's multiple alternative GRM rubrics against reward hacking; K3's agentic generative reward model (mandatory protocol: read output, generate rubric, score each candidate, write a scorepad; tournament-style group reward from binary comparisons; verbosity guard where a candidate longer than sigma * l0 loses); DeepSeek-V3.2's per-prompt rubric GRM; DeepSeek-V4's GRM trained jointly with the actor serving as its own judge and no scalar reward models; Qwen3's three reward types over more than 20 tasks (rule-based; model-based with reference using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct; model-based without reference using a preference RM); R1's own use of a generative RM for SFT data and a preference-model reward only in the last 400 steps of stage 2; process vs outcome at RL scale. Out: preference RMs (Module 4), AI-labelled data (Module 8), exploitation and defenses (Module 19). After this module the reader can choose among verifier, reference-based judge, rubric GRM and preference RM for a task and name the exploit each invites.
topics: the reward-source ladder: rule-based verifier -> reference-based model judge -> rubric-guided generative RM -> preference RM, by precision, coverage and hackability
Rubrics as Rewards: instance-specific rubric feedback as reward; smaller judges work better with rubrics; gains vs direct Likert LLM-judge rewards (authors' numbers, abstract-only)
Kimi K2: self-critic pairwise reward (the model judges its own outputs), closed-loop critic refinement on verifiable-reward rollouts, an explicit rubric per synthesized task
Kimi K2.5: multiple alternative GRM rubrics to limit overfitting to one preference signal

Kimi K3's agentic GRM: judge protocol (read, generate rubric, score each candidate, scorepad), tournament-style group reward from binary comparisons (worked example), verbosity guard (candidate longer than sigma * l0 loses)
DeepSeek-V3.2: generative RM with per-prompt rubrics for general tasks versus rule-based outcome rewards (plus length penalty and language consistency) for reasoning and agent tasks
DeepSeek-V4: no scalar reward models; rubric-guided RL data; RL applied to the GRM itself; the actor is the GRM; claimed benefit of joint optimisation with minimal human annotation
Qwen3 general RL: >20 tasks; rule-based, model-based with reference (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge), model-based without reference (preference RM); why rule-based is kept (precision, prevents hacking)
R1: generative RM (DeepSeek-V3) to judge part of the SFT data; preference-model reward confined to the final 400 of 1,700 stage-2 steps because longer exposure caused hacking
process vs outcome at RL scale: R1's PRM failure modes (Supp. G.2), Llama 3's stepwise RMs for trace filtering, step credit without a PRM via GiGPO (forward pointer to Module 18)
reported limits: open problem of tasks without a reliable verifier (R1 Supp. G.1); judge bias toward length and the guards used against it
disagreements: Learned reward models, verifiers, or generative/rubric judges? (primary)
Process vs outcome supervision (secondary: R1's PRM failure at scale; Llama 3's use for filtering)

modules.title: RL Environments for LLMs: Task Datasets, Harnesses, Verifiers, State, and Reward Shaping
modules.description: What an RL environment is for an LLM (from Gymnasium's reset/step to NeMo Gym's tasks + harness + verifier + state), how labs synthesize them at scale, and why harness diversity matters.
modules.scope: In: the classical environment interface (Gymnasium: reset returns (observation, info); step returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info)) and what changes for an LLM (observation = text or tool output, action = token sequence or tool call, episode = trajectory); NeMo Gym's definition of an environment as dataset of tasks + agent harness + verifier + per-task state, with reward shapes in its examples (Blackjack +1/0/-1, Bird SQL binary by unordered result-set equality, GUI coordinate quadratic reward by Euclidean distance, multi-reward tutorials); OpenEnv (Gymnasium-style API over WebSocket, Docker isolation, MCP tools at /mcp, 40+ environments, 'early development'); Reasoning Gym (>100 procedural generators with adjustable difficulty, performance cliffs, adaptive curricula); environment synthesis in reports (K2: 3,000+ real MCP tools and 20,000+ evolved synthetic tools with a rubric per task; V3.2: 1,800+ environments and 85,000 prompts; GLM-5: 10K+ SWE environments plus terminal and multi-hop search; Nemotron 3 Ultra's list and released environments); K3's white-box composable harness. Out: sandbox and serving design (System Design course Modules 27, 37), multi-turn credit assignment (Module 18), exploits (Module 19). The OpenEnv, NeMo Gym and Gymnasium facts are unversioned snapshots via extraction: mark them as such. Environment design is the least comparatively documented part of the stack: reports describe their environments but do not ablate them, and the module must say so. After this module the reader can specify an environment (tasks, harness, verifier, state, reward) for a new domain and name what to test before trusting it.
topics: Gymnasium interface: Env as an MDP class; reset -> (observation, info); step -> (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info); terminated (task done or failed) vs truncated (time limit)

the LLM translation: observation = text/tool result, action = generated tokens or a tool call, episode = trajectory, reward at the end or per step; what the 'state' is when the sandbox holds the real state
NeMo Gym anatomy: dataset of tasks, agent harness, verifier, per-task state; trainer-agnostic (NeMo RL, Unsloth, VeRL); v0.7.0 snapshot caveat
reward-shape catalogue from shipped examples: sparse +1/0/-1, binary by result equality, smooth quadratic by distance, multi-reward composition

OpenEnv: Gymnasium-style API over WebSocket (sync or async), Docker image per environment (local, cloud sandbox, HF Space), MCP environments at /mcp, 40+ environments, training integrations (TRL, SkyRL, torchforge, Unsloth, others), maturity warning

Reasoning Gym: >100 task generators and verifiers; unlimited data with adjustable difficulty; sharp cliffs as difficulty rises; adaptive curricula beat fixed difficulty; RLVR generalises within a domain

environment synthesis at scale: K2 (3,000+ MCP tools from GitHub plus 20,000+ evolved synthetic tools, thousands of agents, rubric and LLM-judge filtering), V3.2 (1,800+ environments, 85,000 prompts), GLM-5 (10K+ SWE environments, terminal, search)

harness diversity: Nemotron 3 Ultra's multi-environment list and harness variation to avoid overfitting to one harness; K3's white-box harness configured from composable modules (tools, prompts, context policy, skills, memory, subagents)

modules.title: On-Policy Distillation as Dense-Reward RL: Per-Token Reverse KL, Cost Arithmetic, and When It Beats RL
modules.description: Why sampling from the student and scoring every token against a teacher gives a dense on-policy signal that plugs into an RL trainer, and the reported cost and capability comparisons with RL.
modules.scope: In: the on/off-policy x sparse/dense taxonomy (SFT off-policy dense; RL on-policy sparse; OPD on-policy dense); the objective (per-token reverse KL to the teacher along the student's own trajectory; discount zero; advantage = negative reverse KL so it reuses the RL trainer); Thinking Machines' Qwen3-8B-Base student with a Qwen3-32B teacher (~70% AIME'24 in ~150 steps vs SFT needing ~2M prompts extrapolated; 9x/18x/30x cost reductions depending on accounting; self-distillation to recover behaviour after mid-training in <10 steps vs 70 for RL); the information-theoretic argument (RL transmits a fixed number of bits per episode, distillation O(N)); Qwen3's strong-to-weak pipeline (off-policy then on-policy) at ~1/10 the GPU-hours of the four-stage pipeline, and Table 21 (17,920 vs 1,800 GPU-hours = 9.96x, derived); R1's observation that RL on Qwen2.5-32B for 10K+ steps only matched QwQ-32B-Preview while distilling R1 did better; ProRL's counter-evidence; the caveats the blog itself states (sampled-token reverse KL only, no seeds, SFT baseline mismatch 60% vs 55.0, models retired in a June 2026 update so numbers may not reproduce). After this module the reader can implement OPD on top of an RL trainer and say when distillation, not RL, is the cheaper route.

modules.title: Calibration-Aware RL: Proper Scoring Rules, the RLCR Reward, and Why Binary Rewards Teach Guessing
modules.description: How binary-reward RLVR degrades calibration and encourages guessing, and how bounded strictly proper scoring rules (Brier) repair it, with the benchmark-grading counter-view.

modules.title: Case Study: Llama 3 and Tulu 3 (2024) - DPO-First Post-Training, the PPO Comparison, and the Birth of RLVR
modules.description: Two 2024 recipes that chose DPO over PPO for preference tuning, and how Tulu 3 added verifiable-reward RL for the skills that have answers.
modules.scope: In: Llama 3 (Meta, 31 Jul 2024): the stated stance of simple post-training (SFT, rejection sampling, DPO) over RL algorithms that are 'less stable and harder to scale'; PPO tried and found to need more compute and do worse on IFEval; six rounds of preference-and-SFT data collection with recent best models; DPO hyperparameters, NLL term, token masking; rejection sampling with PagedAttention >2x throughput; stepwise RMs for trace filtering. Tulu 3 (Ai2, 22 Nov 2024): SFT -> length-normalized DPO -> RLVR; the measured PPO-vs-DPO cost (about 28 h on two nodes vs about 4 h on one) and the decision to use DPO for preference iteration and PPO for RLVR; RLVR definition; value model initialised from a general RM; KL 0.05/0.07; asynchronous PPO with vLLM on Ray; 405B on MATH only, >5 MATH points in 25 steps, stopped at 75 steps; limitations (value-free GRPO untested). This module reads each recipe stage by stage; mechanisms are referenced to Modules 4-10, not re-derived. Pipeline plumbing is cross-referenced to the System Design course Module 36. Out: the reasoning-RL era (Modules 27 onward). After this module the reader can state what each 2024 recipe optimised and what made the field move to GRPO-style RLVR in 2025.

Llama 3 DPO details: lr 1e-5, beta 0.1, NLL coefficient 0.2 on chosen sequences, masked formatting tokens, six rounds of recent-model preference data
Llama 3 rejection sampling with PagedAttention (>2x throughput) and reward-model/stepwise-RM filtering for reasoning traces

Tulu 3 RLVR: verification function reward on GSM8K, MATH, IFEval-style constraints; value model from a general RM; KL 0.05 (8B) / 0.07 (70B); asynchronous PPO with vLLM via Ray
scaling to 405B: MATH-only RLVR, >5 MATH points within 25 steps, 75 steps total because of infrastructure difficulty

modules.title: Case Study: DeepSeek-R1 - R1-Zero, the Four-Stage R1 Pipeline, Its Compute, and What the Nature Version Changed
modules.description: The mandatory case study, read stage by stage: GRPO from DeepSeekMath, R1-Zero's rule-based RL, the four-stage R1 pipeline, reported costs, failed attempts, and later critiques.
modules.scope: In: the lineage (TRPO -> PPO -> GRPO in DeepSeekMath, Feb 2024; R1 on 22 Jan 2025 on the same day as Kimi k1.5; Tulu 3's RLVR coinage earlier; o1-preview Sep 2024 attested only via Lambert's bibliography because the OpenAI page returned HTTP 403: say so); R1-Zero (RL on DeepSeek-V3-Base, accuracy + format rewards, lr 3e-6, KL 0.001, T = 1, 16 samples, max length 32,768 then 65,536 at step 8.2k, 10,400 steps, 512 outputs per step, rollout of 8,192 outputs in 16 minibatches, reference replaced every 400 steps; AIME 2024 15.6 -> 77.9% in v2 and -> 71.0% in v1, with the version stated every time); R1's stages (cold start; reasoning RL with a language-consistency reward and the unexplained clip epsilon 10; rejection-sampling SFT of ~600k reasoning + ~200k non-reasoning samples; second RL of 1,700 steps with a preference model only in the last 400); compute (R1-Zero 101K GPU-h/$202K, R1 41K, total 147K GPU-h/$294K, the 80 h vs 'about 4 days' inconsistency); distillation vs small-model RL (Qwen2.5-32B); failed attempts (PRM, MCTS); critiques (Dr. GRPO's aha-in-base, Spurious Rewards, Yue et al.); Nature publication details (Nature 645:633-638, 17 Sep 2025) known from search results only: mark unverified. topics: lineage and corrections: TRPO (2015) -> PPO (2017) -> GRPO (DeepSeekMath, 2024) -> R1; RLVR term from Tulu 3 (22 Nov 2024); o1-preview (Sep 2024) attested only second-hand; R1 and k1.5 same day

R1-Zero schedule arithmetic: 10,400 steps (1.6 epochs); 32 questions x 16 = 512 outputs/step; 8,192 outputs per rollout = 16 minibatches, one inner epoch; reference replaced every 400 steps
R1-Zero results and the version issue: AIME 2024 pass@1 15.6 -> 77.9% (v2, expanded Nature version) vs 71.0% (v1); 86.7% with self-consistency/majority vote; state which version each number is from
problems that motivated R1: poor readability, language mixing, narrow reasoning-only RL

R1 four stages: cold-start SFT; stage-1 reasoning RL with the language-consistency reward (and the printed clip epsilon 10, unexplained); rejection-sampling SFT with ~600k reasoning (correct only, some judged by a generative RM via V3) + ~200k non-reasoning; stage-2 RL of 1,700 steps with preference reward only in the last 400

modules.title: Case Study: Kimi k1.5 to K3 - Mirror-Descent Policy Optimization, Self-Critic Rewards, Token-Budget RL, and Nine-Expert MOPD
modules.description: Four Moonshot AI reports (Jan 2025 to Aug 2026) read as one lineage: a non-GRPO objective, agentic environment synthesis, log-ratio masking, Toggle, PARL, and the K3 expert-then-distill pipeline.
modules.scope: In: Kimi k1.5 (22 Jan 2025): no MCTS, value function or PRM; online policy mirror descent with a sampled-mean baseline and squared-error surrogate; length reward warm-up; curriculum and prioritized sampling; partial rollouts; long2short; headline results (77.5 AIME, 96.2 MATH-500, 94th percentile Codeforces, 74.9 MathVista). K2 (28 Jul 2025; v2 3 Feb 2026): K1.5 algorithm reused; Gym-like RL framework; self-critic pairwise rubric reward with closed-loop critic refinement; budget control; temperature decay; PTX loss; agentic synthesis (3,000+ MCP tools, 20,000+ synthetic). K2.5 (2 Feb 2026; v2 7 Aug 2026): token-level log-ratio mask independent of advantage sign, Toggle, PARL, multiple GRM rubrics, zero-vision SFT. K3 (27 Jul 2026; v2 7 Aug 2026): SFT -> 9 domain-by-effort experts via RL -> MOPD; partial rollouts with staleness delegated to per-token regularization; effort RL; agentic GRM judge; verbosity guard; white-box environment. Mechanisms are referenced to Modules 9, 12, 16, 18, 22, 23, not re-derived. Out: Kimi infrastructure details beyond what the reports state. After this module the reader can trace how each Kimi design choice answered the failure of the previous generation. The reports were read in part (abstract, selected sections): the writer fetches full text before citing sections not listed in the source map.
topics: k1.5 design stance: simple RL framework without MCTS, value functions or PRMs; objective as online policy mirror descent with the current model as reference; mean-reward baseline; squared-error surrogate

k1.5 training recipe: curriculum easy-first plus prioritized sampling toward low success; length reward per problem, warmed up; partial rollouts for long responses; long2short (merging, shortest rejection sampling, DPO, RL)
k1.5 results: 77.5 AIME, 96.2 MATH-500, 94th percentile Codeforces, 74.9 MathVista; same release day as R1
K2: reuse of the K1.5 optimiser; Gym-like framework; prompt difficulty by SFT-model pass@k; self-critic rubric reward and closed-loop critic refinement; budget control; temperature decay; PTX loss
K2 agentic data and environments: 3,000+ real MCP tools plus 20,000+ evolved synthetic tools, rubric per task, LLM-judge filtering

K2.5: gradient mask on tokens with log-ratio outside [alpha, beta] independent of advantage sign, introduced to bound the off-policy divergence caused by training-vs-inference framework discrepancies; multiple GRM rubrics; Toggle (-25 to -30% tokens); PARL; zero-vision SFT
K3 pipeline: SFT -> domain experts at varying reasoning effort (3 domains x 3 efforts {low, high, max}) -> MOPD; scaling RL FLOPs improves knowledge, reasoning, vision, agent and coding capability

K3 RL details: partial rollouts (pause when fraction lambda of trajectories completes; staleness across policy versions); effort RL via budgets (reward -1 beyond tau * b0, tau annealed); agentic GRM protocol; verbosity guard; white-box composable environment

Importance ratio and clipping: token-level, sequence-level, IS-weight clipping, or soft gating? (applied: K2.5 and K3)

Controlling response length / reasoning effort (applied: k1.5 length reward through K3 effort experts)

modules.title: Case Study: Qwen3 - Four-Stage Reasoning Pipeline, 3,995 Query-Verifier Pairs, Thinking-Mode Fusion, and Strong-to-Weak Distillation
modules.description: Alibaba's Qwen3 post-training recipe: a long-CoT cold start, a deliberately tiny reasoning-RL set, mode fusion, general RL over 20+ tasks, and a distillation route for small models that cost about a tenth of the GPU hours.
modules.scope: In: the flagship four stages (long-CoT cold start; reasoning RL with GRPO on 3,995 query-verifier pairs with large batch, many rollouts per query and off-policy training; thinking-mode fusion; general RL); the query-verifier selection criteria; general RL's reward system over more than 20 tasks and its three reward types (rule-based; model-based with reference using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as judge; model-based without reference using a preference RM) and why rule-based rewards are kept; agent training with multi-turn rollouts and real execution feedback; strong-to-weak distillation (off-policy then on-policy) for small models at about 1/10 the GPU hours; Table 21 for Qwen3-8B (RL: AIME'24 67.6, AIME'25 55.5, pass@64 unchanged at 90.0/83.3, 17,920 GPU-hours; on-policy distillation: 74.4/65.5, pass@64 93.3/86.7, 1,800 GPU-hours); the follow-up GSPO algorithm from the same team (Module 12) as related work, not claimed to be Qwen3's optimiser. modules.title: Case Study: DeepSeek-V3.2 to V4 - Scaling GRPO Past 10% of Pre-Training Compute, Then Replacing Mixed RL with On-Policy Distillation
modules.description: What changed from R1 to V3.2 (stability fixes, mixed RL, rubric GRM, synthesized agent environments) and from V3.2 to V4 (specialists plus multi-teacher OPD, jointly trained GRM, three effort modes).
modules.scope: In: DeepSeek-V3.2 (2 Dec 2025): specialist distillation then mixed RL (reasoning, agent and alignment merged into one GRPO stage to avoid catastrophic forgetting); rewards (rule-based outcome + length penalty + language consistency; per-prompt rubric GRM for general tasks); the stability toolbox (advantage R - mean(R); unbiased KL estimate via importance ratio with domain-dependent KL; off-policy sequence masking; Keep Routing for MoE; Keep Sampling Mask); post-training budget >10% of pretraining cost; 1,800+ environments and 85,000 prompts; V3.2-Speciale. DeepSeek-V4 (arXiv id 2606.19348; the arXiv API shows published 2026-04-26, unexplained: cite by title and id, do not date from the id): same pipeline with mixed RL replaced by OPD from >10 teachers, per-domain GRPO specialists, GRM trained jointly with the actor, three reasoning-effort modes, full-vocabulary OPD. After this module the reader can say which R1 choices DeepSeek revised and why, and what V4 gave up by dropping mixed RL.

V3.2 rewards: rule-based outcome + length penalty + language consistency for reasoning and agent; GRM with per-prompt rubrics for general tasks; contrast with R1's stance against neural RMs

modules.title: Case Study: Olmo 3 - OlmoRL, RL-Zero from a Fully Open Base, and Measured Rollout Economics
modules.description: The only fully open recipe with measured infrastructure numbers: OlmoRL's list of GRPO modifications, offline and active difficulty filtering, the 1,000-second step, continuous batching, and RL-Zero as a contamination-free testbed.
modules.scope: In: OlmoRL as GRPO plus zero-gradient filtering, active sampling, token-level loss, no KL loss, clip-higher, truncated importance sampling and no std normalization, and the reason each is there; offline difficulty filtering (drop prompts with pass rate above 62.5%; the 32B run relies on active sampling); the rollout economics (rollouts up to 32K tokens, average over 10K, mean 14,628 as used in the waste arithmetic; the 32B run's 8 H100 training nodes and 20 inference nodes; learner waiting 75% of the time; ~5x GPU use for inference vs training, ~14x at 7B; continuous batching and inflight updates giving 2x speed on half the GPUs, 7B 15 -> 6 days; a 1,000 s step with 125 s of training, so generation needs >8x speedup before training bottlenecks; ~54% static-batching waste, derived); RL-Zero (open-weight bases with undisclosed mid-training data can contaminate RLVR benchmarks; Olmo 3 releases RL-Zero from a fully open base with decontaminated data). The researcher read the RL sections only: the writer fetches the SFT, DPO and data sections before covering them, and may narrow to the RL recipe. Out: pretraining. After this module the reader can reproduce the economics of a rollout-bound RL run from Olmo 3's published numbers.
topics: OlmoRL as a diff against GRPO: each of the seven modifications and its rationale

no-std advantage to remove difficulty bias; token-level loss normalised over all tokens in the batch to avoid length bias; no KL; clip-higher; truncated importance sampling following Yao et al. (second-hand)
difficulty control: offline filter at pass rate > 62.5%; active sampling for the 32B run
rollout economics: up to 32K tokens (average >10K), 8 training nodes + 20 inference nodes (32B), learner waits 75%, ~5x inference GPUs vs training (7B: ~14x)
static vs continuous batching: (32K - 14,628)/32K ~ 54% waste (derived); continuous batching + inflight updates: 2x faster on half the GPUs; 7B ~15 days -> ~6 days (Table 23)
step-time decomposition: 1,000 s average step with 125 s training; generation would need >8x speedup to make training the bottleneck (footnote arithmetic)
RL-Zero: why open-weight bases with undisclosed mid-training data can contaminate RLVR evaluation; fully open base plus decontaminated RL data
relation to Tulu 3's recipe and to Spurious Rewards (contamination makes spurious signals look real)
what the writer must fetch before covering the SFT and DPO stages (not read by the researcher)

modules.title: Case Study: GLM-5 and Nemotron 3 Ultra - Asynchronous Agentic RL, Deterministic Indexer Top-k, Environments the Report Calls Open, and the Limits of MOPD
modules.description: Two 2026 agent-era recipes: GLM-5's three RL stages with cross-stage distillation and its determinism fix, and Nemotron 3 Ultra's unified RLVR across many environments followed by MOPD, with its stated limits.
modules.scope: In: GLM-5 (17 Feb 2026; v2 24 Feb): three RL stages with on-policy cross-stage distillation; reasoning RL as GRPO + IcePop with the KL term removed; the sparse-attention indexer determinism finding (non-deterministic CUDA/TileLang top-k caused drastic degradation after a few RL steps with an entropy drop; torch.topk fixed it; indexer frozen; replaying k = 2048 indices judged impractical vs MoE routing replay); asynchronous agentic RL with a Multi-Task Rollout Orchestrator, TITO gateway and Direct Double-sided Importance Sampling; 10K+ SWE environments plus terminal and multi-hop search. Nemotron 3 Ultra (12 Jun 2026): one unified RLVR run across terminal, office, SWE, search, tool-calling, math, code, STEM, safety, chat, instruction following, long-context QA and structured outputs; asynchronous GRPO with stability optimisations, global batch 8,192 with 16 rollouts per sample, 48K then 64K max generation; harness diversity; MOPD from >10 teachers with dense per-token rewards, asynchronous; its reported limitation (end-to-end agentic rollouts in MOPD cause large inefficiency; single-turn PivotRL-style rollouts used instead; whether end-to-end would gain more is open); release of recipes, data and environments. Mechanisms referenced to Modules 14, 17, 18, 22. Out: architecture details (hybrid Mamba-Transformer, DSA) beyond RL impact. After this module the reader can state what each lab found that the other did not.

modules.title: Choosing a Method: PPO, DPO, GRPO-Family, On-Policy Distillation, and Hybrids Under Reward, Data, Compute, and Stability Constraints
modules.description: A decision framework tying each algorithm to the constraint it was built for, with the evidence (and its strength) behind each cell.
modules.scope: In: the constraint axes: reward type (pairwise preference, verifier, judge-only), available data (pairs vs prompts), generation compute and critic memory, stability and tuning burden, target (chat alignment, reasoning, agent), model size (small: distill; large: RL), multi-skill integration, calibration need. Each recommendation cites the report that supports it, states the stack and scale in which it was measured, and marks evidence strength (single report, replicated, conflicting). Covers: preference tuning (DPO vs PPO evidence: Llama 3, Tulu 3, Xu et al., Ivison et al.; data quality dominating); reasoning with verifiers (GRPO family; the default recipes in TRL, Olmo 3, ScaleRL, DAPO and what they agree on: no KL, token-level or prompt-level aggregation, clip-higher or CISPO, mismatch correction); agentic coding (sandbox verifiers, async RL, harness diversity); small models (distillation first, per Qwen3 and R1); non-verifiable tasks (rubric GRM, K3 protocol); multi-skill targets (mixed RL vs MOPD); calibrated outputs (RLCR-style Brier term, Module 24). Cells with no source are stated as no source. This module is a synthesis, not an assessment or a deliverable. Out: new disagreements. modules.title: The Frontier as of October 2026: Open Problems, Moving Parts, and What Closed Labs Do and Do Not Disclose
modules.description: A dated map of what is settled, contested and open in RL post-training, with the leading indicators in the sources and a bounded account of what closed labs have actually put on the record.
modules.scope: In: a dated settled/contested/open map across the course's mechanisms (e.g. no-KL and token-level loss are near consensus in open recipes; sharpen-vs-expand, MOPD adoption, train-inference fixes, agentic rollouts under MOPD, tasks without verifiers (R1 Supp. G.1), environment quality, calibration, the RLCD claim remain open); the 2026 shift Lambert documents (MOPD popular; expert counts; labs not unanimous); time-stamped milestones from DeepSeekMath (Feb 2024) to the October 2026 reports; a bounded section on closed labs, using only their own primary statements already in the map (OpenAI papers S3, S6, S28, S33; Anthropic papers S7, S29), plus pointer-only items the writer must fetch first (the gpt-oss model card: 'similar CoT RL techniques as OpenAI o3', low/medium/high levels, no direct optimisation pressure on the CoT; Baker et al. on CoT monitoring) and an explicit statement that no primary recipe was found for o1/o3, Claude or Gemini (the o1 page returned HTTP 403); no rumoured recipes. This is a section of this module and not a separate module because the source map supports no more than that. Also: the as-of notes (version and date ambiguities) and what to watch. Out: any unsourced prediction (the writer labels forecasts as the writer's own and keeps them few). After this module the reader knows which parts of this course are likely to be revised first and where the evidence is weakest.
topics: settled/contested/open map by mechanism with module numbers and the sources behind each cell

emerging consensus in open recipes: no KL, token- or prompt-level aggregation, clip-higher or CISPO-type weights, mismatch correction, active/dynamic sampling (Olmo 3, DAPO, GLM-5, Magistral pointer, ScaleRL)

open questions the reports themselves state: tasks without verifiers (R1 G.1), MOPD for long-horizon agentic rollouts (Nemotron), whether RL expands capability (Modules 20, 21), whether RL scaling continues to pay (Module 15)
the 2026 recipe shift: MOPD as a merging tool (MiMo-V2-Flash first, then Nemotron >10, K3 nine, V4 >10), 'labs are far from unanimous'
reasoning-effort as a trained product surface (K3 low/high/max, V4 three modes, gpt-oss low/medium/high pointer)
calibration as a post-training target: RLCR/behavioural calibration in the literature and the unpublished RLCD claim (Modules 24, 25)

closed-lab disclosures, bounded: what OpenAI and Anthropic have published in the map (S3, S6, S28, S33; S7, S29), pointer-only items to fetch first, and the explicit list of what is not disclosed; no rumours
date and version hygiene: R1 v1 vs v2 numbers, V4 id vs date, Lambert edition dates, unversioned docs snapshots; what must be re-checked first when the course is revisited
leading indicators and what to watch, each with its source (new open recipes with released environments, MOPD ablations, mismatch fixes, scaling-fit extrapolations)
disagreements: Does RLVR create new reasoning capability, or only sharpen what the base model can already do? (open)
How to combine many skills: single mixed RL, sequential stages, or specialists + on-policy distillation? (open)
RL or distillation for strong small reasoning models? (open)
Calibration: train it into the policy, or fix how benchmarks grade? (open)
TypeSafe "RLCD": new post-training regime, or a rebranding of known calibration-aware RL? (open, claim-only)
